question.stem: After running `use schoolDB` followed by `db.students.insertOne({ name: "Aditi", age: 18 })`, which state changes have occurred on the MongoDB server (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `schoolDB` remains hidden from `show dbs` until a second document is inserted
options.B: `schoolDB` now physically exists on disk and appears in `show dbs`
options.C: The `students` collection must still be created manually using `db.createCollection("students")`
options.D: The inserted document lacks an `_id` field because none was provided in `insertOne()`

answer.explanation: Inserting the first document `{ name: "Aditi", age: 18 }` into `db.students` automatically creates the `students` collection so it appears in `show collections` (E) and materializes `schoolDB` on disk so it appears in `show dbs` (B). (Key Takeaway: A single `insertOne()` call materializes both the target collection and the selected database.)

question.stem: Which queries validly use comparison or array membership operators to filter documents in `db.students` (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.find({ age: { $gte: 18 } })`
options.B: `db.students.find({ age: $in[17, 18, 19] })`
options.C: `db.students.find({ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } })`
options.D: `db.students.find({ age: { $ne: 17 } })`

answer.explanation: In MongoDB query filters, comparison operators (`$gte`, `$in`, `$ne`) are placed inside a nested object attached to the field name: `{ age: { $gte: 18 } }` (A), `{ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } }` (C), and `{ age: { $ne: 17 } }` (D). Options B and E violate BSON operator nesting syntax. (Key Takeaway: Comparison operators must be nested inside the target field's filter object `{ <field>: { <operator>: <value> } }`.)

question.stem: How do `db.students.find({ age: 18 })` and `db.students.findOne({ age: 18 })` differ when multiple documents have `age: 18` (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `find({ age: 18 })` returns a cursor over all matching documents, whereas `findOne({ age: 18 })` returns only the first matching document object
options.B: `findOne({ age: 18 })` supports chaining `.sort()` and `.limit()`, whereas `find({ age: 18 })` does not
options.C: `find({ age: 18 })` supports chaining `.sort()`, `.skip()`, and `.limit()`, whereas `findOne({ age: 18 })` does not support cursor methods directly
options.D: `findOne({ age: 18 })` rejects projection arguments, whereas `find({ age: 18 })` accepts them

answer.explanation: `find()` returns an iterable cursor yielding all matching documents and supports cursor methods `.sort()`, `.skip()`, and `.limit()` (A, C). `findOne()` returns a single document object directly and does not support cursor methods (though both support projection as a second argument). (Key Takeaway: `find()` returns a chainable cursor for all matches; `findOne()` returns a single document object without cursor methods.)

question.stem: Consider `db.students.find({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 })`; which operational behaviors occur during its execution (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Documents with `grade: 8` are excluded because `$gte` tests strict inequality
options.B: Documents with `grade: 8`, `grade: 9`, or `grade: 10` satisfy the first filter argument
options.C: The `name` and `grade` fields are explicitly included in every returned document
options.D: The `_id` primary key field is suppressed from every returned document
options.E: Other unmentioned fields such as `subjects` or `promoted` are omitted from the output

answer.explanation: `$gte: 8` matches grades 8 and higher (B). The inclusion projection `{ name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 }` includes `name` and `grade` (C), suppresses `_id` via `_id: 0` (D), and excludes all other unmentioned fields like `subjects` (E). (Key Takeaway: An inclusion projection with `_id: 0` emits strictly the fields marked `1`.)

question.stem: Which single command increments `attempts` by `1` and appends `"History"` to `subjects` for the first student named `"Rahul"` (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $set: { attempts: 1 }, $pull: { subjects: "History" } })`
options.B: `db.students.updateMany({ name: "Rahul" }, { $inc: { attempts: 1 }, $push: { subjects: "History" } })`
options.C: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $inc: { attempts: 1 }, $push: { subjects: "History" } })`
options.D: `db.students.insertOne({ name: "Rahul", $inc: { attempts: 1 }, $push: { subjects: "History" } })`

answer.explanation: Targeting only the first matching student requires `updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, ...)`, incrementing a numeric field uses `$inc: { attempts: 1 }`, and appending an element to an array uses `$push: { subjects: "History" }` (C). (Key Takeaway: Pair `updateOne()` with `$inc` for numeric addition and `$push` for array appending.)

question.stem: When executing `db.students.find({ $or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] })`, which documents from `students` will be returned (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `{ name: "Rahul", age: 17 }`
options.B: `{ name: "Meera", age: 17 }`
options.C: `{ name: "Kabir", age: 18 }`
options.D: `{ name: "Aditi", age: 18 }`

answer.explanation: The `$or` filter matches any document where either `age >= 19` OR `name == "Rahul"`. `{ name: "Rahul", age: 17 }` matches the second clause (A), and `{ name: "Vikram", age: 20 }` matches the first clause (E). Documents with `age < 19` and `name != "Rahul"` fail both clauses. (Key Takeaway: `$or` includes documents satisfying at least one branch of its condition array.)

question.stem: Which statements accurately compare `db.students.deleteMany({})` and `db.students.drop()` when cleaning up data (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Both commands remove secondary indexes defined on `students`
options.B: `db.students.deleteMany({})` removes every document in `students`
options.C: `db.students.drop()` retains the empty `students` collection in `show collections`
options.D: `db.students.deleteMany({})` leaves the `students` collection container intact
options.E: `db.students.drop()` permanently deletes the `students` collection, its documents, and its indexes

answer.explanation: `db.students.deleteMany({})` deletes all documents (B) without dropping the collection container or its indexes (D), whereas `db.students.drop()` permanently removes the collection container, all documents, and all indexes (E). (Key Takeaway: `deleteMany({})` empties data in place; `drop()` destroys the collection and its indexes.)

question.stem: What happens when `db.students.updateMany({ age: 18 }, { $set: { promoted: true } })` executes against a collection where some `{ age: 18 }` documents do not yet have a `promoted` field (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Documents lacking the `promoted` field are skipped by `updateMany()`
options.B: Existing fields such as `name` and `age` are erased from matching documents
options.C: Every document with `age: 18` is updated across the entire collection
options.D: `$set` adds `{ promoted: true }` to matching documents lacking the field and updates it on those that already have it

answer.explanation: `updateMany()` applies the update to every document matching `{ age: 18 }` (C), and the `$set` operator sets the value of `promoted` to `true` (creating the field if absent) while preserving all other fields like `name` and `age` (D). (Key Takeaway: `updateMany()` with `$set` creates or updates the target field across all matching documents.)

question.stem: Which operations in the MongoDB shell are permanent and cannot be undone once executed (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Deleting the active database via `db.dropDatabase()`
options.B: Dropping a collection and its indexes via `db.students.drop()`
options.C: Removing a single matched document via `db.students.deleteOne({ name: "Kabir" })`
options.D: Removing multiple matched documents via `db.students.deleteMany({ age: 17 })`

answer.explanation: All five destructive operations — `db.dropDatabase()` (A), `db.<collection>.drop()` (B), `deleteOne()` (C), filtered `deleteMany()` (D), and empty-filter `deleteMany({})` (E) — permanently remove data from the storage engine and cannot be undone without external backups. (Key Takeaway: Database drops, collection drops, and document deletions are irreversible in MongoDB.)

question.stem: In `db.students.find().sort({ age: 1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`, which roles are performed by the chained cursor methods (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `sort({ age: 1 })` orders all matching documents from lowest to highest `age`
options.B: `skip(10)` omits the first 10 documents from the ordered result sequence
options.C: `limit(5)` restricts each document to at most 5 fields
options.D: `skip(10)` deletes the first 10 documents from the `students` collection on disk
options.E: `limit(5)` caps the maximum number of documents returned by the cursor to 5

answer.explanation: In a pagination pipeline, `sort({ age: 1 })` orders documents in ascending order (A), `skip(10)` omits the first 10 results (B), and `limit(5)` caps the number of returned documents at 5 (E). Neither `skip()` nor `limit()` modifies disk data or restricts field counts. (Key Takeaway: `sort()`, `skip()`, and `limit()` transform cursor output order, offset, and page size.)
